units.question: I'm reading up on Kyrgyzstan before a trip. What is its capital, roughly how many people live there, and just how mountainous is the land?
units.gold: Kyrgyzstan's capital is Bishkek. The population is about 6.2 million (6,219,751, 2025 estimate), spread over roughly 200,000 sq km (199,951 sq km). The country is landlocked and almost entirely mountainous, dominated by the Tien Shan range: 94% of its territory lies above 1,000 m and the average elevation is about 2,750 m, with many high peaks, glaciers and alpine lakes. Most people live in rural areas, with the densest settlement in the north around Bishkek and around Osh in the west.
rubric: 94% of the land above 1,000 m; average elevation about 2,750 m (Tien Shan)
Penalize: naming Osh or another city as the capital, or a population off by more than 1 million

units.question: How big is Malta, what is its capital, and how many of its islands have permanent residents?
units.gold: Malta is a small archipelago of 316 sq km, a little less than twice the size of Washington, D.C. Its capital is Valletta. Only the three largest islands are inhabited: Malta itself, Gozo (Ghawdex) and Comino (Kemmuna); the rest are uninhabited. About 522,000 people live in the country (2025 estimate), most of them on the eastern half of the main island of Malta.

Penalize: saying all islands are inhabited or giving a capital other than Valletta

units.question: Give me the head count and the capital of the Cocos (Keeling) Islands, and tell me which of the islands people actually live on.
units.gold: The Cocos (Keeling) Islands, an Australian territory in the Indian Ocean, are tiny: about 14 sq km of land and only 593 residents (2021 estimate). The capital is West Island. The group has 27 coral islands, mostly arranged as a horseshoe-shaped atoll around a lagoon, with North Keeling lying about 30 km away, but only two islands are populated: Home Island and West Island.
rubric: Only Home Island and West Island are populated
Penalize: a population in the thousands or naming Home Island as the capital
units.answer: The Cocos (Keeling) Islands have a population of around 600 people, with West Island and Home Island being inhabited [1]. The capital is West Island [5].
units.sources:
[1] Cocos (Keeling) Islands (cited)
The territory's dual name (official since the islands' incorporation into Australia in 1955) reflects that the islands have historically been known as either the Cocos Islands or the Keeling Islands, the latter of which is still a common short name. The territory consists of two atolls made up of 27 coral islands, of which only two – West Island and Home Island – are inhabited. The population of around 600 people consists mainly of Cocos Malays, who mostly practise Sunni Islam and speak a dialect of Malay as their first language.

The islands are generally considered to be the southernmost point of Asia.

units.question: A friend told me Bhutan's capital got its name from a legend. Which city is it, how many people live in Bhutan, and what's the story?
units.gold: Bhutan's capital is Thimphu. The country has about 893,000 people (892,877, 2025 estimate) on 38,394 sq km. The origin of the name is not certain, but the traditional explanation, going back to the 14th century, says 'thim' means dissolve and 'phu' means rock: a local deity is said to have dissolved before a traveller's eyes and become part of the rock on which the city now stands.

units.question: Who is Curacao's capital city named after, and roughly how large is the island in land and people?

The island covers 444 sq km, a bit more than twice the size of Washington, D.C., and has about 153,000 inhabitants (2024 estimate). Most people live in and around Willemstad, which has about 144,000 people.

units.question: How did the Mauritian economy grow out of its plantation past, and what currency and income level does the island have now?
units.gold: Mauritius was built as a sugar economy: from 1722 the French ran profitable sugar-cane plantations worked by enslaved Africans, and after abolition in 1835 the British brought contract labourers from the Indian subcontinent. Since independence in 1968 it has stayed a stable democracy, attracted heavy foreign investment and now has one of Africa's highest per capita incomes, about $27,300 real GDP per head (2024). Sugar milling, textiles and tourism remain key industries. The currency is the Mauritian rupee (MUR).

units.question: I'm confused about who runs Western Sahara. Who controls it today, and why did the planned independence vote never happen?
units.gold: Western Sahara is a non-self-governing territory whose sovereignty is unresolved. After Spain left its colony in 1976, Morocco annexed the northern two-thirds and later claimed the rest when Mauritania withdrew in 1979. A guerrilla war with the Polisario Front ended in a 1991 ceasefire and a UN peacekeeping operation. The UN planned a referendum offering independence or integration with Morocco, but it never took place because the sides could not agree on who was eligible to vote. Morocco controls about three-quarters of the territory, west of a 1,600 km sand berm.

Spain attempted to transfer its administration to Morocco and Mauritania despite an advisory opinion of the International Court of Justice that those countries had no sovereignty over Western Sahara; a war erupted and the pro-independence Polisario Front proclaimed the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic (SADR). Mauritania withdrew its claims in 1979, and Morocco secured de facto control of most of the territory, including all major cities and most natural resources. The SADR established a government-in-exile in Tindouf, Algeria.

[3] Polisario Front
History > Founding: The Polisario Front was founded on May 10 1973, by a group of Sahrawi students and activists. At the time, Western Sahara was under Spanish control. The group began in Mauritania but had supporters throughout Western Sahara. Their objective was to fight for independence and to put an end to Spanish Colonial Rule. The first military action taken by the Polisario Front took place on May 20 1973, when they attacked a Spanish military post. This date is remembered as the beginning of their armed struggle.

[4] Polisario Front
History > Founding > Spanish withdrawal and regional conflict: In 1975. after many years of pressure, the Spanish Government agreed to withdraw from Western Sahara. Instead of granting it independence, Spain signed the Madrid Accords, granting control over the territory over to Morocco and Mauritania. units.question: When and by what process did Eritrea become independent, and who has led the country since then?
units.gold: Eritrea became independent from Ethiopia on 24 May 1993. Ethiopia had annexed it as a province in 1962, starting a 30-year armed struggle that ended in 1991 when Eritrean fighters defeated government forces; Eritreans then overwhelmingly approved independence in a 1993 referendum. Isaias Afwerki has been the only president since independence, and his rule has been highly autocratic, with indefinite mandatory national service.

units.question: Summarize when Trinidad and Tobago became independent and from whom, and name the industry that has dominated its economy for more than a century.
units.gold: Trinidad and Tobago gained independence from the United Kingdom on 31 August 1962 and is a parliamentary republic. Oil was discovered on Trinidad in 1910 and petroleum remains the dominant industry; together with natural gas production and processing it has made the country one of the most prosperous in the Caribbean. units.question: We want to hike near volcanoes in New Zealand. Which natural hazards there should we be aware of?
units.gold: New Zealand has frequent earthquakes, though they are usually not severe, and significant volcanism on the North Island. Ruapehu (2,797 m) has had large eruptions within the past century, and Taranaki could produce dangerous avalanches and lahars (volcanic mudflows). Other historically active volcanoes include Okataina, Raoul Island, Tongariro and White Island. The climate is temperate with sharp regional contrasts.

units.answer: New Zealand's natural hazards include earthquakes and volcanic activity, with Ruapehu and other volcanoes posing risks [1]. Always follow safety guidelines and heed evacuation orders if warned about volcanic activity.

units.question: Why does Guatemala face both volcanic and storm risks, and which of its volcanoes stand out?
units.gold: Guatemala lies on the Pacific Ring of Fire, the belt holding about 75% of the world's volcanoes and up to 90% of its earthquakes, so its mountains contain many volcanoes and it suffers occasional violent earthquakes. Its Caribbean coast is highly exposed to hurricanes and tropical storms. Notable volcanoes include Pacaya, one of the most active with frequent eruptions since 1965, Santa Maria, named a Decade Volcano for its explosive history, and Fuego; Tajumulco (4,220 m) is the highest point in Central America.

units.question: Explain what the volcano on Montserrat did to the island's capital and its people from the mid-1990s on.
units.gold: The Soufriere Hills volcano on Montserrat began erupting in 1995 and devastated much of the island; about two-thirds of the population left for abroad. A massive eruption in 1997 destroyed most of the capital, Plymouth, and left about half of the island uninhabitable. Volcanic activity continued for years, with the last eruption in 2013. The island also faces severe hurricanes from June to November.
rubric: Two-thirds of the population fled abroad
Penalize: saying the capital was unaffected or confusing the island with another Caribbean territory

units.question: Which mother tongues are most common in Pakistan, and what part does English play there?
units.gold: By mother tongue, Punjabi is the largest language in Pakistan at about 38.8%, followed by Pashto (18.2%), Sindhi (14.6%), Saraiki (12.2%) and Urdu (7.1%), with smaller shares of Balochi, Hindko and Brahui. Mahajirs/Mohajir/Muhajir () constitute about 8 percent of the population. They are Muslims who settled in Pakistan after the end of British India in 1947. units.question: Compare the Maldives and the Seychelles on how high their land rises and which natural hazards each one faces.
units.gold: The Maldives is extremely low-lying: its highest point is just 5 m (a golf-course tee on Villingi Island) and its mean elevation about 2 m, so it is exposed to tsunamis and very sensitive to sea level rise. The Seychelles is much higher, rising to 905 m at Morne Seychellois. It lies outside the cyclone belt, so severe storms are rare, and its main hazard is occasional short droughts.

units.question: I'm choosing between living in Austria or Ireland. Which one produces more per person, and how do their landscapes compare in height?
units.gold: Ireland's real GDP per capita is much higher: about $115,300 in 2024 versus about $63,300 for Austria. Their terrain is very different. Austria is mostly mountainous (the Alps cover the west and south), with a mean elevation of about 910 m and hazards such as landslides and avalanches, while Ireland is low-lying, with a mean elevation of about 118 m and its highest point, Carrauntoohil, at 1,041 m.

[3] As a young person in Austria, what steps should I take so that I can buy a house someday
Answers > Answer (score 2): Given your income, expenses and the provided property prices, you don't need to do much to afford a house. Just leaving the money in your bank account while you save should be enough to afford a house in your area within 5 years, even if you had no pay raise.

For the rest, ask your bank, and go to a second one to see what they suggest. I don't think any other place makes sense because they will not provide a better / cheaper offering and you need a bank for your loan anyways. A bank can show you ways to save money in a secure way, explain if a so called Bausparer is beneficial, can help with funding (Kredit) and know details about potential tax benefits and state funded support (cheaper loans etc). Your local bank will also know the local housing market well.

[4] As a young person in Austria, what steps should I take so that I can buy a house someday
Answers > Answer (score 2): - Don't buy stocks, (bond) ETFs, funds: chances are you may actually make a lot of money in 5 years, but it may also drop 30% - 40% just before you would want to buy a house
- Try to get a good interest rate on a term deposit (Spareinlage / Sparbuch in Austria; the latter likely has higher fees, so try to avoid it). 20.000 at 3% for five years will return about 23.185. in total, you will be way above the required 80k at the time of writing if you save 20k per year, for 5 years, and get interest. Realistically, it will be around 110k.
- Alternatively, buy bonds (Anleihen) from companies with a low chance of default. They should pay about 4 percent interest at the time of writing. Make sure they expire at a time you want to start to look for houses on the market(e.g. in 5 years).

With regards to the housing market, the market conditions don't matter too much. It's difficult to predict what will happen. Also, you cannot buy now, and you don't want to wait too long either it seems.
